questions.q: A wheel turns through 3.5 complete revolutions. What is its angular displacement in radians?
questions.exp: One revolution is 2π rad, so θ = (2π)(3.5) = 22.0 rad. The value 1260 is the displacement in degrees. The deck works with radians because s = rθ and v = ωr hold only when θ is in radians.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Angle in radians’

questions.q: A turntable rotates at 45 revolutions per minute. What is its angular speed in rad/s?
questions.exp: ω = (45 rev/min)(2π rad/rev)(1 min/60 s) = 4.71 rad/s. The value 283 forgets to convert minutes to seconds, and 0.750 is the frequency in revolutions per second, not an angular speed in rad/s.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Angular velocity and angular acceleration’ and ‘Toolkit 1’

questions.q: A wheel of radius 0.35 m turns at a constant angular speed of 12.0 rad/s. What is the speed of a point on its rim?
questions.exp: For a point at distance r from the axis, v = ωr = (12.0)(0.35) = 4.20 m/s. Dividing gives 34.3, which does not have the units of speed. The value 50.4 is the radial acceleration, ω²r, in m/s².
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Toolkit 2: linking linear and angular motion’

questions.q: A point on the rim of a wheel of radius 0.50 m moves with angular speed 3.0 rad/s while the wheel is speeding up with an angular acceleration of 8.0 rad/s². What is the magnitude of the total acceleration of the point?
questions.exp: The tangential acceleration is a<sub>t</sub> = αr = 4.00 m/s² and the radial acceleration is a<sub>rad</sub> = ω²r = 4.50 m/s². These are perpendicular, so a = √(a<sub>t</sub>² + a<sub>rad</sub>²) = 6.02 m/s². Adding the magnitudes, 8.50 m/s², is wrong because the components are at right angles.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Lecturer example: a point on a speeding-up wheel’ and ‘A point on a speeding-up wheel: solution’

questions.q: Two points on a wheel that rotates about a fixed axis are at distances of 0.10 m and 0.30 m from the axis. Which statement about their motion is correct?
options: They have the same linear speed, and the outer point has the greater angular speed.
They have the same angular speed, and the outer point has the greater linear speed.
They have the same linear speed and the same angular speed.
They have the same angular speed and the same linear speed, because they are on the same wheel.
questions.exp: Every point of a rigid rotating body turns through the same angle in the same time, so all points have the same ω. The linear speed v = ωr is proportional to the distance r from the axis, so the outer point is faster.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Two points on one wheel’

questions.q: A washing-machine drum spinning at 40.0 rad/s is braked with a constant angular deceleration until it stops after 8.0 s. How many revolutions does the drum make while stopping?
questions.exp: With constant α, θ = ½(ω₀ + ω)t = ½(40.0 + 0)(8.0) = 160 rad. One revolution is 2π rad, so the number of revolutions is 160/(2π) = 25.5 rev. The value 160 is the angle in radians, not revolutions.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Lecturer example: a braking washing-machine drum’ and ‘Toolkit 1’

questions.q: On an ω–t graph the angular velocity falls along a straight line from 10 rad/s at t = 0 to −6.0 rad/s at t = 4.0 s. What is the angular acceleration?
questions.exp: The slope of an ω–t graph is the angular acceleration: α = Δω/Δt = (−6.0 − 10)/4.0 = −4.00 rad/s². The sign is negative because ω decreases. The wheel first slows, stops at t = 2.50 s, and then turns in the opposite direction with increasing speed.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Concept check: reading an ω(t) graph’ and ‘Reading an ω(t) graph: answers’

questions.q: Two small masses are attached to a light rod that rotates about a fixed axis: 1.0 kg at 0.20 m from the axis and 3.0 kg at 0.50 m from the axis. What is the moment of inertia about the axis?
questions.exp: For separate particles I = Σmr² = (1.0)(0.20)² + (3.0)(0.50)² = 0.790 kg·m². The distance is squared, so the mass farther from the axis dominates. Using mr gives 1.70, which has the wrong units.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Kinetic energy of rotation and the moment of inertia’ and ‘Toolkit 3: moment of inertia’

questions.q: A uniform thin rod of mass 2.0 kg and length 1.20 m has I<sub>cm</sub> = ML²/12 about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to the rod. What is its moment of inertia about a parallel axis through one end?
questions.exp: Use the parallel-axis theorem: I = I<sub>cm</sub> + Md², with d = L/2 = 0.60 m. Then I = 0.240 + (2.0)(0.60)² = 0.960 kg·m², which equals ML²/3. The end of the rod is farther from the axis than the centre, so I about the end is larger than I<sub>cm</sub> = 0.240 kg·m².
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘The parallel-axis theorem’ and ‘Lecturer example: one body, three axes’

questions.q: A hoop and a uniform solid disc have the same mass and the same radius. Each turns about a central axis perpendicular to its plane. Which has the greater moment of inertia, and why?
options: The hoop, because all of its mass is at the full radius from the axis
The disc, because it has more material near the centre
They are equal, because the mass and the radius are equal
The disc, because it has the larger area
questions.exp: I = Σmr² grows when mass sits farther from the axis. A hoop has I = MR², while a solid disc has I = ½MR², because part of the disc’s mass is closer to the axis. The moment of inertia depends on how the mass is distributed, not only on M and R.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘An opening question: the disc and the hoop’ and ‘Moments of inertia of standard bodies’

questions.q: A force of 25.0 N is applied at a point 0.40 m from a pivot. The angle between the force and the line from the pivot to the point is 30°. What is the magnitude of the torque about the pivot?
questions.exp: Torque has magnitude τ = rF sin φ, where φ is the angle between r and F: τ = (0.40)(25.0) sin 30° = 5.00 N·m. Only the component of the force perpendicular to r produces torque. Using cosine, or dropping the angle, gives the wrong values 8.66 and 10.0 N·m.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Torque’ and ‘Toolkit 4: torque’

questions.q: Torque and energy both have SI units of newton metres. Which statement is correct?
options: Torque is a scalar, so it can be added to energies directly.
Torque is a vector related to turning about an axis, and it is not an energy, so it is not expressed in joules.
Torque and energy are the same quantity, so the unit joule is used for both.
Torque is an energy, because force times distance is energy.
questions.exp: Energy is a scalar, the work done by a force over a displacement. Torque is a vector given by r × F, with r and F perpendicular in the useful case, and it describes the tendency to change rotation. The unit N·m is the same, but the joule is reserved for energy and work, so torque is written in N·m.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Torque and energy are different quantities’

questions.q: A cord wound round a uniform solid disc of mass 4.0 kg and radius 0.30 m is pulled with a constant force of 6.0 N tangent to the rim. The disc turns about its central axis. What is its angular acceleration?
questions.exp: Use Στ = Iα. The torque is τ = FR = 1.80 N·m and for a solid disc I = ½MR² = 0.180 kg·m². So α = τ/I = 10.0 rad/s². Using I = MR², the value for a hoop, gives 5.00. The value 1.50 is the linear acceleration F/M, not an angular one.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Toolkit 5: rotational dynamics’ and ‘Lecturer example: pulling a cord wound on a disc’

questions.q: A 3.0 kg mass hangs from a light cord wound round a pulley, which is a uniform solid disc of mass 2.0 kg and radius 0.10 m. The pulley turns freely about its axis and the cord does not slip. What is the acceleration of the hanging mass?
questions.exp: For the mass, mg − T = ma. For the pulley, TR = Iα with I = ½MR² and α = a/R, so T = ½Ma. Adding the equations gives mg = (m + ½M)a, so a = mg/(m + ½M) = 7.35 m/s². The acceleration is less than g because the pulley has to be spun up. Treating the pulley mass as if it were all in the load, mg/(m + M), gives 5.88 m/s².
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Lecturer example: a mass on a cord turns a pulley’ and ‘The pulley: Newton’s laws for the acceleration’

questions.q: A constant torque of 40.0 N·m turns a flywheel through 3.0 revolutions. How much work does the torque do?
questions.exp: For a constant torque, W = τθ with θ in radians. Here θ = (2π)(3.0) = 18.8 rad, so W = (40.0)(18.8) = 754 J. Using the number of revolutions, 3.0, instead of radians gives 120 J, and using degrees gives 43200 J. Both are wrong.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Work and power of a torque’ and ‘Lecturer example: a flywheel under a constant torque’

questions.q: A uniform solid disc of mass 1.5 kg and radius 0.20 m spins about its central axis at 30.0 rad/s. What is its rotational kinetic energy?
questions.exp: First I = ½MR² = ½(1.5)(0.20)² = 0.0300 kg·m². Then K = ½Iω² = ½(0.0300)(30.0)² = 13.5 J. Omitting the ½ gives 27.0 J, and Iω = 0.900 kg·m²/s is the angular momentum, not an energy.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Kinetic energy of rotation and the moment of inertia’ and ‘Toolkit 6’

questions.q: A solid sphere, a solid disc and a hoop, all of the same mass and radius, are released together from rest at the top of an incline and roll without slipping. In what order do they reach the bottom?
options: They arrive together, because they have the same mass and radius
The hoop first, then the disc, then the sphere
The sphere first, then the disc, then the hoop
The disc first, then the sphere, then the hoop
questions.exp: Rolling without slipping shares the energy between translation and rotation: K = ½Mv² + ½Iω² with ω = v/R. A body with a smaller I/(MR²) puts less energy into rotation and so gains more translational speed. The ratios are 2/5 for the sphere, 1/2 for the disc and 1 for the hoop. The mass and radius cancel.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Concept check: a race down an incline’ and ‘The race: solution’

questions.q: A solid sphere rolls without slipping from rest down a slope, falling through a height of 1.20 m. What is its speed at the bottom? For a solid sphere I = (2/5)MR².
questions.exp: Energy conservation with rolling: Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Iω² = ½Mv² + ½(2/5)MR²(v/R)² = (7/10)Mv². So v = √(10gh/7) = 4.10 m/s. The value 4.85 m/s would be the speed of a block sliding without friction, with no rotational energy. The value 3.96 m/s would be for a solid disc.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Energy with rotation, and rolling’ and ‘Your turn: a sphere rolls up an incline’

questions.q: A skater spinning on ice pulls her arms in close to her body. Her angular speed increases. What happens to her rotational kinetic energy?
options: It stays the same, because angular momentum is conserved.
It decreases, because the moment of inertia decreases.
It increases by creating energy from nothing.
It increases, because the skater does work in pulling her arms in.
questions.exp: With no external torque, L = Iω is constant. As I decreases, ω increases in proportion. K = L²/(2I), so K rises when I falls. The extra energy comes from the work done by the skater’s muscles as she pulls her arms inward. Angular momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Concept check: a skater pulls in her arms’ and ‘Conservation of angular momentum’

questions.q: A merry-go-round with moment of inertia 200 kg·m² turns at 1.50 rad/s. A 30 kg child, initially at rest, jumps on at a distance of 2.0 m from the axis. What is the new angular speed? Neglect friction at the bearing.
questions.exp: There is no external torque about the axis, so L = Iω is conserved: I₁ω₁ = (I₁ + mr²)ω₂. Then ω₂ = (200)(1.50)/(200 + (30.0)(2.00)²) = 0.938 rad/s. The child adds mr² = 120 kg·m² to the moment of inertia, so the speed decreases. Leaving the distance squared out of the child’s term gives wrong values.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Your turn: a child jumps on a merry-go-round’ and ‘Toolkit 7: angular momentum and its conservation’

questions.q: The velocity of a 500 g particle at the point r = (4î + 3ĵ − 2k̂) m is v = (5î − 2ĵ + 4k̂) m s<sup>−1</sup>. What is the angular momentum of the particle about the origin?
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Your turn: a child jumps on a merry-go-round’ and ‘Toolkit 7: angular momentum and its conservation’

questions.q: An engine develops a power of 1600π W at constant torque of 40 N m. Determine the angular velocity of the engine in revolutions per minute.
questions.exp: P = τω gives ω = 1600π/40 = 40π rad s<sup>−1</sup> = 20 rev s<sup>−1</sup> = 1200 rev min<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Work and power of a torque’ and ‘Lecturer example: a flywheel under a constant torque’

questions.q: A DVD has an initial angular velocity of 23.5 rad s<sup>−1</sup> and acceleration of −6 rad s<sup>−2</sup> as it slows to stop. A point on the edge of the disc is connected by a line to the centre of the disc. Determine what angle the line sweeps after 1.2 s.
questions.exp: θ = ω<sub>0</sub>t + ½αt² = (23.5)(1.2) + ½(−6)(1.2)² = 28.2 − 4.32 = 23.9 rad. (The DVD stops only at t = 23.5/6 = 3.9 s, so it is still turning at 1.2 s.)
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Lecturer example: a braking washing-machine drum’ and ‘Toolkit 1’

questions.q: The instantaneous angular position θ of a rotating disk at any time t is given by θ = (2 rad s<sup>−2</sup>)t² + (6 rad s<sup>−1</sup>)t and the diameter of the rotating disk is 0.20 m. Find the distance a particle on the rim of the rotating disk travels in 2 s.
questions.exp: Angle turned in 2 s: θ(2) − θ(0) = 2(4) + 6(2) = 20 rad. The rim distance is s = rθ = (0.10 m)(20 rad) = 2.0 m.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Toolkit 2: linking linear and angular motion’

questions.q: The instantaneous angular position of a rotating disk is θ = (2 rad s<sup>−2</sup>)t² + (6 rad s<sup>−1</sup>)t. What is the value of the angular acceleration of the disk?
questions.exp: ω = dθ/dt = 4t + 6 and α = dω/dt = 4.0 rad s<sup>−2</sup> (constant).
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Angular velocity and angular acceleration’ and ‘Toolkit 1’

questions.q: The grinder in a corn milling machine has a constant moment of inertia of 0.5 kg m² about its axis of rotation. Its angular speed is ω = (10.0 rad s<sup>−5</sup>)t<sup>4</sup>. Calculate the value of the torque at time t = 3 s.
questions.exp: α = dω/dt = 40t³ = 40(3)³ = 1080 rad s<sup>−2</sup>, so τ = Iα = (0.5)(1080) = 540 N m. The unit of torque is N m, which is kg m² s<sup>−2</sup>. The paper printed kg m² s<sup>−1</sup>, which is a misprint.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Toolkit 5: rotational dynamics’ and ‘Lecturer example: pulling a cord wound on a disc’

questions.q:
A force is applied on a body making it turn about a point O. The torque of the force depends on
I. the magnitude of the applied force.
II. the perpendicular distance from O to the point of application of the force.
III. the shortest distance from O to the line of action of the force.
questions.exp: τ = F·d<sub>⊥</sub> where d<sub>⊥</sub> is the shortest (perpendicular) distance from O to the line of action of the force (III). The perpendicular distance from O to the point of application (II) is not what enters the torque; the distance to the point is r, and τ = rF sin φ.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Torque’ and ‘Toolkit 4: torque’

questions.q: A roller in a printing press turns through an angle θ(t) given by θ(t) = βt<sup>2</sup> − γt<sup>3</sup>, where β = 3.20 rad s<sup>−2</sup> and γ = 0.500 rad s<sup>−3</sup>. At what time does the maximum positive angular velocity occur?
questions.exp: ω = dθ/dt = 2βt − 3γt². It is a maximum when α = dω/dt = 2β − 6γt = 0, so t = β/(3γ) = 3.20/1.50 = 2.13 s (α changes from positive to negative there, so it is a maximum: ω<sub>max</sub> = 3.41 rad s<sup>−1</sup>).
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Angular velocity and angular acceleration’ and ‘Toolkit 1’

questions.q: A flywheel is made of iron (density 7800 kg m<sup>−3</sup>) in the shape of a 10.0 cm thick uniform disk. What would be the diameter of such a disk if it is to store 10.0 MJ of kinetic energy when spinning at 9.42 rad s<sup>−1</sup> about an axis perpendicular to the disk at its centre? [Hint: I = ½mR² for a disk with the axis at the centre.]
questions.exp: K = ½Iω² = ¼mR²ω² with m = ρπR²h, so K = ¼ρπhR⁴ω². R⁴ = 4K/(ρπhω²) = 4(1.00×10<sup>7</sup>)/[(7800)(3.14)(0.100)(9.42)²] = 183.7 m⁴, R = 3.68 m and the diameter is 7.36 m (π = 3.14 as given on the paper).
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Kinetic energy of rotation and the moment of inertia’ and ‘Toolkit 3: moment of inertia’

questions.q: An iron flywheel (density 7800 kg m<sup>−3</sup>) is a 10.0 cm thick uniform disk that stores 10.0 MJ of kinetic energy when spinning at 9.42 rad s<sup>−1</sup>. What is the radial acceleration of a point on its rim when it spins at this rate?
questions.exp: a<sub>r</sub> = ω²R = (9.42)²(3.68) = 327 m s<sup>−2</sup>, using R = 3.68 m from Question 26.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Toolkit 2: linking linear and angular motion’

questions.q: A 3.00 kg piece of metal rotates about a point O. At a point P it has a velocity of magnitude 12.0 m s<sup>−1</sup>, directed horizontally to the right. P is 8.00 m from O, up and to the left of O along a line that makes 36.9° with the horizontal. If the only force acting on the piece of metal is its weight, what is the rate of change (magnitude and direction) of its angular momentum about O at this instant? (Directions are given relative to the page, which shows the plane of the motion.)
options: 115 kg m² s<sup>−2</sup>, into the page
179 kg m² s<sup>−2</sup>, into the page
188 kg m² s<sup>−2</sup>, into the page
188 kg m² s<sup>−2</sup>, out of the page
questions.exp: dL/dt = τ = r × w. With r = 8.00 m at 36.9° above the horizontal (to the left of O), the horizontal lever arm is 8.00 cos 36.9° = 6.40 m, so τ = (3.00)(9.81)(6.40) = 188 N m. The weight points down and the lever arm is to the left, so r × w points out of the page (right-hand rule).
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Torque’ and ‘Toolkit 4: torque’

questions.q: A 3.00 kg piece of metal rotates about a point O. At a point P it has a velocity of magnitude 12.0 m s<sup>−1</sup>, directed horizontally to the right. P is 8.00 m from O, up and to the left of O along a line that makes 36.9° with the horizontal. The only force on the piece of metal is its weight. By considering the directions of the angular momentum L about O and its rate of change dL/dt, we can conclude that
options: the magnitude of the angular momentum is decreasing.
the magnitude of the angular momentum is increasing.
the magnitude of the angular momentum remains constant.
the gravity force is accelerating the piece of metal upward.
questions.exp: L points into the page and dL/dt points out of the page, so they are opposite and the magnitude of L is decreasing (d|L|²/dt = 2L·dL/dt < 0). Gravity can only accelerate the piece of metal downward, not upward.
questions.ref: Lecture 8 deck, slide ‘Your turn: a child jumps on a merry-go-round’ and ‘Toolkit 7: angular momentum and its conservation’
